USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the May 10 List 3 hike at 25% and the May 15 Huawei restriction in place, and do not implement the proposed List 4 on the remaining ~$300B of consumer-heavy imports. Do not roll back tariffs or offer purchase/structural concessions after Beijing stripped law-change language from the draft. Leave the USTR comment/hearing process running as unused leverage and accept talks only if China restores enforceable commitments; use farm-aid as a domestic bridge through June rather than another tariff round this week.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is elevated but not high. After April talks that reported progress on text and enforcement, China sent back a draft that deleted commitments to change laws on IP theft, forced tech transfer, competition policy, financial-services access, and currency (Reuters, 10 May). That walk-back is a direct hit to the U.S. structural objective, not a symmetric bargaining hiccup. List 3 then rose from 10% to 25% on 10 May; China answered on 13 May by raising duties on its ~$60B U.S. list (many effective 1 June), concentrated on agriculture and related goods already hit since 2018. Farm-belt cash flow is the clearest U.S. vulnerability—soy exports to China collapsed after the 25% levy, soybean prices fell, and the White House is already talking ~$15B in offset aid—so the dispute is biting a politically salient export sector. Markets are flagging risk: the 10-year yield fell to 2.37% on 15 May (−69 bp in the window), VIX jumped to 20.55 on 13 May, and CNY weakened from ~6.73 to 6.87 in the first half of May. That is not an existential shock: Michigan sentiment is at 100, CPI is contained, and China’s IP and reserves are still stable, so the U.S. economy is not in a tariff recession. The unused List 4 (apparel, footwear, laptops, consumer electronics; hearing 17 June; earliest ~24 June) plus the Huawei entity listing give Washington remaining leverage, which is why the score is well below the +0.5 “high” anchor. Action should be hold, not more escalation: two large U.S. moves landed in five days (List 3 rate hike and EO 13873/Huawei). Implementing List 4 now would tax consumer goods and, on Trade Partnership-type estimates cited around the USTR notice, could take ~1% off GDP if China matches—while rewarding China’s text deletions with a rollback would collapse U.S. enforcement credibility. Mnuchin said no further talks were scheduled “for now”; the right stance is to sit on the new posture, let the June 1 Chinese hike and the List 4 comment record arrive, and reopen negotiation only on the pre-walk-back legal text.
key_factors: China deleted law-change commitments on IP, tech transfer, competition, financial access, and currency in the early-May draft
List 3 already at 25% (10 May); China’s $60B retaliation scheduled 1 June, aimed at U.S. agriculture
Huawei entity-list / EO 13873 just imposed (15 May)—further non-tariff escalation this week would stack shocks
Proposed List 4 (~$300B consumer goods) is only in the comment process; earliest implementation late June
U.S. real economy still resilient (UMCSENT 100) but rates/VIX and farm cash flow show rising cost of a longer war
CNY depreciation and stable Chinese reserves/IP mean Beijing is not yet overextended enough to force a cheap U.S. concession

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the already-announced 1 June rate hike on the existing ~$60B U.S. list in force as the proportionate answer to the 10 May List 3 increase, but do not add a new tariff list or fire an immediate non-tariff blast (rare earths, Treasury sales, mass licensing delays) in response to yesterday’s Huawei order. Invite Lighthizer/Mnuchin back to Beijing and keep a G20/Osaka channel open, without new legal-change, unilateral-enforcement, or purchase concessions while Washington is still hiking and blacklisting. Use the weeks before 1 June and before any $300B list is finalized to test whether the U.S. will trade a pause for talks; if Commerce actually severs Huawei’s U.S. supply, reserve a calibrated non-tariff response then.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is high, not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is now ~$250B at 25% after List 3 rose from 10% to 25% on 10 May, and the White House has directed preparation of tariffs on the remaining ~$300B (timeline 2019-05-05, 2019-05-10). That is a material hit to export hubs. The 15 May EO 13873 plus Commerce’s move to put Huawei and ~70 affiliates on the Entity List is firm-level targeting of a national champion and a direct strike on tech self-sufficiency (timeline 2019-05-15; Reuters/Skadden). The yuan has already slipped from ~6.73 in early May to 6.8742 on 15 May, with spot prints near 6.90 and talk of 7 — FX pressure is real (DEXCHUS; Reuters 13 May). Morgan Stanley’s contemporaneous estimate that the latest hike could trim ~0.5pp of Chinese growth (up to ~1pp if the $300B list lands) sits next to the +0.5 CHN threat anchor (major export sectors, FX, Huawei, unemployment risk). It is not +1.0: industrial production is still +5.0% YoY, reserves are ~$3.12T and slightly up, merchandise exports remain large, and the discount rate is unchanged — no financial-stability break yet (CHNPRINTO01IXPYM, TRESEGCNM052N, XTEXVA01CNM667S).

Action should not automatically escalate. China already announced the mirror tariff move on 13 May (5–25% on ~$60B, mostly 1 June), and Beijing is running out of U.S. goods to tax. A further blast after the Huawei order would likely accelerate the remaining $300B list and deepen the growth/FX hit, while conceding on enforceable legal changes or large extra purchases would reward coercion after Washington hiked mid-talks (Liu He: remove extra tariffs, balanced text, purchases tied to real demand; talks called a “small setback,” door still open). Negotiate without new commitments is the stance that answers the tariff hike, keeps a path off the $300B cliff, and does not pretend Huawei is costless.

Real economy not broken: IP ~+5% YoY, reserves ~$3.12T, exports still large
Further non-tariff escalation risks bringing the $300B list forward; concession now rewards mid-talks coercion
